summary: Describes using ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption in the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

eli5.summary: How to use a popular lock-and-seal method inside secure messages.

subtitle: How to use the ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated cipher inside CMS authenticated-enveloped data.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) needed conventions for using the ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption algorithm in its authenticated-enveloped-data content type.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8103 assigns an algorithm identifier, requires a 12-octet nonce in the parameters field, maps the AEAD inputs and outputs to the AuthEnvelopedData fields, and defines an S/MIME capabilities encoding.
tldr.outcome: CMS messages can be encrypted and integrity-protected in one step with ChaCha20-Poly1305, as long as a nonce is never reused with the same key.

today: RFC 8103 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2017. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: ChaCha20 and Poly1305
sections.content:
RFC 8103 specifies the conventions for using ChaCha20-Poly1305 authenticated encryption with the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), specifically the authenticated-enveloped-data content type from RFC 5083. CMS itself is defined in RFC 5652.

ChaCha is a stream cipher developed by D. J. Bernstein in 2008, a refinement of Salsa20. ChaCha20 is the 20-round variant and needs a 256-bit key and a 96-bit nonce. Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator that produces a 16-byte tag and needs a 256-bit, single-use key. The text says both were designed for high-performance software implementations, can be implemented with few resources, and were designed to minimize side-channel leakage.
sections.eli5: ChaCha20 scrambles the message so only the right person can read it. Poly1305 adds a little stamp that shows nobody changed it.

sections.title: The AEAD Construction
sections.content:
The two pieces are combined into an Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data (AEAD) algorithm, often called AEAD_CHACHA20_POLY1305 and described in RFC 7539. It takes four inputs: a 256-bit key, a 96-bit nonce, a plaintext of arbitrary length, and arbitrary-length additional authenticated data (AAD). A nonce value cannot be used securely more than once with the same key.

It produces two outputs: ciphertext of the same length as the plaintext, and a 128-bit authentication tag. Decryption mirrors encryption. Poly1305 is run over the AAD and the ciphertext, and the message is authenticated if and only if the calculated and received tags match.
sections.eli5: You put in a secret key, a one-time number, the message and some public notes. Out come a scrambled message and a stamp. To check it later, you recompute the stamp and see if it matches.

sections.title: Key Management and Fresh Keys
sections.content:
Reusing a nonce with the same key destroys the security guarantees, and it can be extremely difficult to use a statically configured key and never repeat a nonce. CMS authenticated-enveloped-data supports four key management techniques that allow a fresh content-authenticated-encryption key for each protected content:

  • Key transport: the fresh key is encrypted in the recipient's public key.
  • Key agreement: the recipient's public key and the sender's private key generate a pairwise key-encryption key, which encrypts the fresh key.
  • Symmetric key-encryption keys: the fresh key is encrypted in a previously distributed key-encryption key.
  • Passwords: the fresh key is encrypted in a key-encryption key derived from a password or other shared secret.

CMS supports other techniques too, but the text says their properties are unknown for this purpose, so designers and implementers must do their own analysis if they use one.
sections.eli5: The safest habit is to make a brand-new key for every message, then lock that key away for the receiver. There are four ways to hand over the key safely.

sections.title: Using It in AuthEnvelopedData
sections.content:
The algorithm identifier goes in the contentEncryptionAlgorithm field of the AuthEnvelopedData EncryptedContentInfo. The algorithm authenticates the attributes in the authAttrs field if present, enciphers the content in encryptedContent, and provides the message authentication code (MAC) in the mac field. The authenticated attributes are DER encoded to form the AAD input. The MAC, called the authentication tag in RFC 7539, protects both authAttrs and encryptedContent. Neither the content nor the AAD needs padding.

The identifier is id-alg-AEADChaCha20Poly1305, an object identifier under the S/MIME algorithms arc ending in 18. The parameters field MUST be present and MUST contain an AEADChaCha20Poly1305Nonce, defined as an OCTET STRING of size 12. Within the scope of any key, the nonce MUST be unique: the set of nonces used with a given key MUST NOT contain duplicates.
sections.eli5: In the message envelope there are named slots for the scrambled content, the public notes and the stamp. This document says which piece goes in which slot, and that every message needs its own one-time number.

sections.title: S/MIME Capabilities
sections.content:
The SMIMECapabilities attribute, defined in RFC 5751, lets software announce a partial list of algorithms it supports. When building a CMS signed-data content type, compliant software MAY include it to announce support for this algorithm.

The SMIMECapability SEQUENCE MUST include the id-alg-AEADChaCha20Poly1305 identifier in the capabilityID field and MUST omit the parameters field. Its DER encoding in hexadecimal is 30 0d 06 0b 2a 86 48 86 f7 0d 01 09 10 03 12.
sections.eli5: A program can tell others, "I know this kind of lock," so people sending it mail know they can use that lock.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA added two entries. In the "SMI Security for S/MIME Algorithms" registry, value 18 is named id-alg-AEADChaCha20Poly1305. In the "SMI Security for S/MIME Module Identifier" registry, value 66 is named id-mod-CMS-AEADChaCha20Poly1305. The appendix of the RFC contains the ASN.1 module with that module identifier.
sections.eli5: The official number lists were updated so this lock and its description each have their own unique number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
CMS AuthEnvelopedData provides the tools to avoid nonce reuse. RFC 7539 explains the stakes: if a nonce is repeated, the one-time Poly1305 key and the keystream are identical between the messages, which reveals the XOR of the plaintexts.

The ciphertext is always the same size as the plaintext, so another mechanism is needed if disclosing the plaintext size is a concern. One invocation can protect 2^32-1 blocks of 64 octets, a total of 247,877,906,880 octets, which the text says is likely sufficient for any CMS content.

The construction is a novel composition of ChaCha20 and Poly1305; a security analysis is given in a paper by Procter. Implementations must randomly generate content-authenticated-encryption keys, because inadequate pseudorandom number generators can leave little or no security. RFC 4086 offers guidance.
sections.eli5: Never use the same one-time number twice with the same key, or secrets leak. Pick keys by truly random choice, and remember the scrambled message is the same length as the original.
